3.0.0.en: 1 And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying, 2 "Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee." 3 So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days' journey. 4 And Jonah began to enter into the city a day's journey, and he cried, and said, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown."

3.0.1.en: Since Jonah had enjoyed life after death, the Lord called him a second time to service, that they too might enjoy life. It is remarkable that God did not rebuke Jonah with a single word, nor wound his feelings because of his flight from the first mission, for the Scripture says:

3.0.2.en: "And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time, saying, Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee. So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days' journey. And Jonah began to enter into the city a day's journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" [1-4].

3.0.3.en: He describes Nineveh in this way: "an exceeding great city of three days' journey." In the literal sense it means that it was a huge city that a man could cross in three days, or that he would keep walking about in its streets for three days. In the spiritual sense, however, Nineveh, as the capital of Assyria, had surrendered itself to Satan and worshipped idols, yet God looks upon it as His great city, which the enemy had seized by its surrendering itself to him. God does not despise His creation, especially man. Even if man turns away from Him, He waits for his salvation and his return to Him, as a great city belonging to Him, in which the Holy Trinity dwells.

3.0.4.en: In our study of the Book of Joshua we saw that the number 3 refers to faith in the Holy Trinity, as it also refers to the Resurrection on the third day. This is the secret of man's greatness, that he becomes the city of God, or as the Scripture calls it, "a city of truth" (Zech 8:3), the kingdom of the Holy Trinity, bearing witness to the Lord's Resurrection by its life raised up in Him.

3.0.5.en: Jonah responded to the call and entered the city a day's journey to proclaim repentance. What is this entering but an indication of the appearing of One of the Holy Trinity, God the Word, who became incarnate and suffered, and so became as one who is in our city? He dwelt in our midst as one of us; through Him we received the work of the Holy Trinity, and we obtained salvation!

3.0.6.en: Jonah cried that after forty days the city of Nineveh would be overthrown, while in the Septuagint it reads: after three days the city of Nineveh will be overthrown. If the number 40 refers to our life in time (which is why the Lord Christ fasted forty days, that we may fast all the days of our life), then Nineveh is overthrown after forty days because heaven and earth pass away so that we may enjoy the new heaven and the new earth. And if the number 3 refers to the Resurrection with the Lord Christ, then the old Nineveh must needs be demolished so that the new one may rise in Him.

3.1.s.en: 2. The faith and repentance of Nineveh:

3.1.0.en: 5 So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them. 6 For word came unto the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and he laid his robe from him, and covered him with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. 7 And he caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, "Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing: let them not feed, nor drink water: 8 But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands. 9 Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?"

3.1.1.en: "So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them" [5].

3.1.2.en: St. Jerome says: [Nineveh believed, but Israel resisted in unbelief. The uncircumcised believed, while the circumcised continued in their unbelief.]

3.1.3.en: The faith of the people of Nineveh was joined to action, so they offered a practical repentance whose weapons were fasting and sackcloth. As St. Jerome says: [Fasting and sackcloth are the weapons of repentance, a help to sinners. Fasting comes first, then sackcloth; the first points to what is unseen and is followed by what is seen. The one stands before the Lord continually, and the other stands for a time before men.] It is as though it befits our repentance to begin with hidden fasting and secret practical life, and only then go forth to outward works.

3.1.4.en: St. Jerome says: [In repentance sackcloth is joined to fasting, so that the empty belly and the garments of mourning entreat the Lord greatly in prayer.]

3.1.5.en: All offered practical repentance to God. The great as well as the small put on sackcloth; the king and the nobles led the procession of repentance, and all the people took part in it, and even the beasts... although Jonah had not given a single word of hope, nor spoken to them of God's love and compassion, nor taught them anything about repentance... Nineveh thus became a wonderful and living example of true repentance.

3.1.6.en: Who is the king who put on sackcloth but the human will, which bows down before God to proclaim its submission to Him and its willingness to become poor for the sake of Him who, being rich, became poor to enrich it? Repentance begins with an inner change in man's will, that is, our inner king. The king took off his royal robe, put on sackcloth and sat in ashes, so that our human will may take off the garments that are the work of its own hands and confess its nakedness and its own poverty. Then the Lord clothes it with His heavenly royal will, grants it the new man who is after His image, raises it from the dunghill to sit with the heavenly ones, and gives the soul a place in the bosom of the Father. As for the nobles, in their repentance they point to the sanctifying of the gifts and abilities we have, that they may work for the kingdom of God. As for the beasts, they point to the body with its energies, which previously walked in darkness in an animal manner. In other words, repentance touches the whole man: his soul and his body, his will and his abilities, his feelings and his conduct!

3.1.7.en: Here it befits us to realize that what drew God's heart to them was neither their fasting in itself nor the sackcloth in itself, but the repentant heart that fasting supported and sackcloth helped. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The people of Nineveh fasted and gained the love of God, whereas the Jews fasted and profited nothing, but rather received blame (Isa 58:3, 7; 1 Cor 9:26). So the danger in fasting is great for those who do not know how they ought to fast. Let us learn the rules of this discipline, so that we may not run in vain or fight as one that beateth the air, or be, in our sorrow, wrestling with shadows. Fasting is a medicine, but it is not always beneficial if it is used in an improper way through the inexperience of those who use it.]

3.2.0.en: What draws our attention in the repentance of the people of Nineveh is their joyful hope. The words of Jonah were few and severe, yet the people of Nineveh did not lose their hope in the merciful Lord. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The message of God on the lips of Jonah was plain; it said nothing about their being received if they returned, yet they proclaimed their repentance, saying: "Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?" [9]. If the Gentiles, who did not understand, were able to grasp this, how much more does it befit us, who have been trained in the divine teachings and have seen many examples of this kind throughout history and in our present experience, to grasp it?!]

3.3.0.en: "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not" [10].

3.3.2.en: First: Repentance does not need a long time but a change of heart. The people of Nineveh were able to seize the mercies of God not through the length of time but through the sincerity of their return to God. Although it befits us to spend all our life in continual, unceasing repentance, longing to reach the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ, this view does not take away from us the awareness of God's mercies, which await the return of every man so as to embrace him at once. St. John Chrysostom says: [Where the fear of God is, there is no need of (many) days nor of the intervention of time; on the contrary, where the fear of God is not, days are of no use... If we cast a rusty vessel into the furnace of the fear of God, it is purified in a short time.]

3.3.3.en: Second: The word "evil" here means the afflictions or chastenings that God allows to come upon man to discipline him or to be an example for others. They are evil in man's eyes, but they are not so in their nature. As Tertullian says: [The Greeks also sometimes use the word "evils" for "afflictions and the harms that befall"]. Father Theodore has confirmed this as well.

3.3.4.en: Third: In former times some stumbled at the Scripture's expression "the Lord repented." Does God change His mind? God uses human language to bring the meaning near to us. God does not repent in the sense of changing His mind; rather it is man who changes his position toward God, so that the judgment concerning him becomes different. When man is stubborn he falls under chastening, and when he turns back from his evil and returns to God he finds Him with open arms. This is what we call repentance! When God issues a sentence of chastening, He does not insist on carrying it out; He issues the sentence so that man may turn from his evil and be pardoned.

3.3.5.en: St. John Chrysostom says in this regard: [In the days of Jonah, had God not threatened destruction, the destruction would not have been removed from them... Had He not threatened us with hell, we would all have fallen into it.] He also says: [The threat of danger causes deliverance from it... The threat of death brings life. The sentence was annulled after it was announced, contrary to what happens among temporal judges, who, once they pass a sentence, it becomes effective... With God, on the contrary, the sentence is announced in order to annul it.]

4.0.0.en: "1 But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry. 2 And he prayed unto the LORD, and said, I pray thee, O LORD, was not this my saying, when I was yet in my country? Therefore I fled before unto Tarshish: for I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentest thee of the evil. 3 Therefore now, O LORD, take, I beseech thee, my life from me; for it is better for me to die than to live. 4 Then said the LORD, Doest thou well to be angry?" [1-4].

4.0.1.en: St. John Chrysostom says: [Truly the prophet was ashamed when he saw that what he had prophesied had not come to pass... But God is not ashamed, seeking one thing only: the salvation of men and the good of His servant.]

4.0.2.en: St. Jerome holds that Jonah's grief and complaint rest on his perception of God's mercies and compassions, for it was not possible for him to present God to the people of Nineveh as a harsh God. Therefore he longed for death, and could not bear to see God's mercies reach the Gentiles while Israel perished. So he says on the prophet's lips: [I alone among the multitude of the prophets announce to my people their destruction through the salvation of others.] These feelings, full of love toward his people, even if they seemed to carry harshness toward the Gentiles, made him ask God to take his life, for his death was better than his life... Jonah repeats the same request once again after the gourd withered, that is, Israel! In any case, this request or desire carried a prophetic aspect: as a representative of the Lord Christ, or as a type of Him, he asks for death on behalf of his people, looking forward to the salvation of mankind being accomplished by the death of the Cross, not by coming down from it or being delivered from it. It is no wonder, then, that the Lord Christ Himself said to His disciples: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you" (Lk 22:15). Since He is the slain Paschal Lamb, He desires to give His life with His own hands, in order to give His believers His Body and Blood, shed for the salvation of the world!

4.0.3.en: Jonah longed to die, but in bitterness because of the perishing of his people, which was made known through the salvation of the Gentiles. But our true Jonah came for this hour, going forward to the sufferings with joy, despising the shame (Heb 12:2), to redeem all mankind.

4.1.0.en: "So Jonah went out of the city, and sat on the east side of the city, and there made him a booth, and sat under it in the shadow, till he might see what would become of the city" [5].

4.1.1.en: Jonah went out of the city, grieved and full of anger, and sat east of the city, watching what the Lord would do to the city. Perhaps Jonah himself represented the Jewish mind, or the elder son who stood outside the house in pain because his younger brother had returned to his father's house (Lk 15:25-31). While the house was full of joy and gladness at the return of the prodigal, the elder son, in his self-righteousness, remained outside the house blaming his father with harsh words.

4.1.2.en: The rebellious city of Nineveh seized the mercies of God through faith working by love, while the prophet Jonah went out of it to set up a booth that was the work of his own hands, that is, his self-righteousness, counting himself better than others and awaiting God's wrath upon them.

4.2.0.en: "6 And the LORD God prepared a gourd, and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shadow over his head, to deliver him from his grief. So Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd. 7 But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered. 8 And it came to pass, when the sun did arise, that God prepared a vehement east wind; and the sun beat upon the head of Jonah, that he fainted, and wished in himself to die, and said, It is better for me to die than to live" [6-8].

4.2.1.en: What did God intend by this gourd, which the Lord God prepared and then prepared a worm to smite it?

4.3.0.en: First: Without doubt the gourd is the Jewish people, of whom the Lord said: "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night" [10].

4.3.1.en: Jonah was exceeding glad of the gourd [6], for he greatly loved his people, but he had no merit in this gourd... He did not plant it, nor tend it, nor watch over it. It was God who raised up Israel and tended him, brought him out of the bondage of Pharaoh, gave him the Law, brought him into the Promised Land and gave him the prophecies, and did not leave him in need of anything. As the Lord rebuked him, saying: "And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it?" (Isa 5:3-4).

4.3.2.en: It befitted Jonah, who represents a small part of one of the branches of this gourd, not to be grieved and angry, for the One who raised up the gourd, chose it and tended it is God Himself, who sent him to Nineveh to shepherd it also through him!

4.3.3.en: He called it "which came up in a night, and perished in a night" [10]. It was not a "son of the day" or a "son of light," but a "son of a night," because it rejected its Savior, the Sun of Righteousness, and loved darkness rather than light. As St. John the Evangelist says: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world... He came unto his own, and his own received him not. But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name" (Jn 1:9-12).

4.3.4.en: Second: God raised up a gourd for Jonah to draw him away from his booth, which was the work of his own hands, as though He were drawing man away from his self-righteousness so that he might enjoy a shade that is from the hand of God, his Creator and Shepherd. But the gourd had to wither, so that in place of this weak plant there might be raised up the wood of the Cross, under which the Church takes shelter to enjoy the joy of the Gospel, saying: "I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste" (Song 2:3).

4.3.5.en: If Jonah went out to the east of the city, awaiting in the spirit of prophecy the rising of the Sun of Righteousness (Mal 4:2), who shines not on Israel alone but on all the Gentiles, then he was exceedingly glad of the gourd because Israel enjoyed the Law and the prophecies to lead him to his Savior. But he was not able to accept Israel's fall as the way for faith to go forth to the Gentiles, and so he was grieved over the withered gourd. He wanted to live under the types and among the shadows of the prophecies as a refuge for himself, and did not realize that they are the way that carries him to the Desire of all nations.

4.3.6.en: If the Law is our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ, as the Apostle Paul says, yet Israel clung to the letter of the Law and the formalities of worship, rejecting the life-giving wood of the Cross.

4.3.7.en: I say: let our souls go forth to the east to enjoy the shining of the Lord upon them; let the gourd of the killing letter wither, that we may enjoy the life-giving Spirit, and receive within us the Desire of all nations as the secret of our enlightenment, our joy and our people!

4.3.8.en: Third: Just as God had spoken to Jonah before through the raging tempest, the tossed ship, the Gentile sailors, the lot and the whale, He now speaks to him through the weak gourd, the east wind and the worm that destroyed the gourd. God speaks at every stage in the language to which man responds and which he understands. When Jonah was in revolt in his heart against God's decision concerning Nineveh, having made the decision to flee, God spoke to him in the language of violence that befits a violent heart. He spoke to him in the language of the tempest so that he might realize his inner turmoil, and in the language of the Gentile sailors so that he might realize that he had gone lame from the spirit of faith. He spoke to him through the ship tossed by the winds so that he might discover his heart, which was about to drift in the midst of the sea of this world, and He spoke with him through the whale so that he might realize the abyss into which he had been swept, the depths that swallowed him, and the prison in which he had placed himself... And now, when Jonah came out frail, with no strength to resist, He spoke to him through the gourd, a weak plant, and the corrupting worm, so that he might realize that he is only a weak plant destroyed by the worm of ingratitude and non-submission.

4.3.9.en: In short, we say that by the language in which the Lord speaks to us we discover our hidden depths.

4.3.10.en: Fourth: St. Hippolytus of Rome sees that the hot east wind which God prepared refers to the Antichrist, who comes out of the east by divine permission to oppose the Church shortly before the Lord's final coming.

4.4.0.en: 9 And God said to Jonah, "Doest thou well to be angry for the gourd?" And he said, "I do well to be angry, even unto death." 10 Then said the LORD, "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: 11 And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?"

4.5.0.en: God concluded His dialogue with Jonah with this beautiful statement: "Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?" [10-11].

4.5.1.en: In this way God reveals His love for mankind, who are the work of His hands.

4.5.2.en: Nineveh, as St. Jerome says, is: [the great city, which is the Church, containing the twelve spiritual tribes who return to childhood in its innocence and simplicity.]
